brief.headline: The two chokepoints have decoupled over the weekend - a concrete Hormuz compromise is now on the table (a mediator says the deal being negotiated centres on Iran running vessel transit with fewer restrictions on ships, with both sides wanting back to the interim ceasefire) while the Red Sea escalated as Houthi missiles and drones hit Aramco facilities at Yanbu and Jizan - and Monday's ring, the first LME session since Friday, is the first price to see any of it, opening onto a curve still in a WIDENING +$14.50 backwardation with stock at a 2022 low of 272,775 t.
bullets: Nothing has moved on the board yet: the LME was shut Saturday and Sunday, so the 24-Jul (Friday) official - cash $3,175.00, 3M $3,160.50, stock 272,775 t - is still the latest published mark and it pre-dates three days of news. Today's official prints 13:20 London. Price sits ~$75 above the $3,085 four-month low: a give-back inside the July rebound, not a break of it.

The Hormuz off-ramp became specific rather than atmospheric. A regional official involved in mediation said a compromise is being negotiated centred on Iran running vessel transit through the Strait with fewer restrictions on ships, and that both the US and Iran want to return to the interim ceasefire; US strikes paused after 13 consecutive nights and Iran-Oman technical talks in Tehran progressed. The qualifiers are real - the US naval blockade of Iranian ports is still enforced (a Mozambique-flagged ship was disabled in the Gulf of Oman on Friday) and Trump has kept the threat of escalation live.

The Red Sea moved the other way, so freight risk is migrating rather than disappearing. After Saudi strikes on Hodeida, the Houthis fired missiles and drones at Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Jizan on Saturday and say they will close Bab el-Mandeb to Saudi-linked shipping - a corridor carrying roughly 12% of world trade, and the route that became more important precisely because Hormuz was disrupted. A Hormuz deal that leaves Bab el-Mandeb contested compresses less of the shipping premium than the headline suggests.

Watch this week: today's official - specifically whether the flat price prices the off-ramp lower WHILE the backwardation widens past +$14.50, which sharpens the squeeze signature rather than relieving it; the five-month mark of the conflict on Tuesday; Netanyahu's Washington visit as a live escalation vector; and on the supply side, the EGA Al Taweelah alumina ramp plus new US primary units behind the tariff wall (Century's Mt Holly expansion, publicly framed as ~+10% of US primary output, and the New Madrid partial restart).

drivers.text: Two chokepoints now moving in OPPOSITE directions - the shipping premium is relocating, not clearing — Hormuz is the compression story: a regional official involved in the mediation says the compromise being negotiated centres on Iran running vessel transit through the Strait with fewer restrictions on ships, both sides want back to the interim ceasefire, US strikes paused after 13 consecutive nights, and Iran-Oman technical talks progressed. Bab el-Mandeb is the offsetting escalation: after Saudi strikes on Hodeida the Houthis hit Aramco facilities at Yanbu and Jizan and restate that the strait - about 12% of world trade, and the fallback route for Gulf cargo since Hormuz was disrupted - is closed to Saudi-linked shipping. Roughly 9% of global primary supply sits behind the Gulf routes an…
drivers.source: AP via Fortune - deal being negotiated centres on Iran running Hormuz vessel transit with fewer restrictions (26-Jul-2026)

drivers.text: US Section 232 at 50% - the tariff leg is ~66% of the US duty-paid premium — Aluminium articles made entirely or almost entirely of aluminium pay 50% on full customs value (derivative aluminium content pays 25%); proclamation 01-Jun-2026, effective 08-Jun-2026 through 31-Dec-2027, CBP guidance CSMS #68855869 - re-verified this run, rate unchanged. At the 24-Jul cash of $3,175 that is ~$1,587.50/t of pure policy cost inside a ~$2,420/t duty-paid premium, leaving ~$832.50/t of residual market premium. A July incentive program lets approved companies investing in US primary capacity import tied metal at half the applicable rate.
drivers.source: White & Case - United States modifies steel, aluminum and copper Section 232 tariffs

drivers.text: New US primary capacity is a medium-term drag on the RESIDUAL US premium — Commerce and South Carolina officials marked Century Aluminum's Mt Holly expansion on 23-Jul, publicly framed as lifting total US domestic primary aluminium output by roughly 10%, with Magnitude 7 Metals restarting part of the New Madrid smelter in Missouri (~75 kt/y). Domestic units displace tariffed imports at the margin, which pressures the ~$832.50/t residual market leg of the US duty-paid premium over time - while leaving the ~$1,587.50/t policy leg entirely untouched. The two components of the US premium are therefore on divergent paths.
drivers.source: GlobeNewswire - Commerce Secretary Lutnick, Senator Scott and Governor McMaster mark ~10% increase in US aluminum production (23-Jul-2026)

drivers.text: Europe: war premium fading against a structural floor — Platts duty-unpaid P1020A in-warehouse Rotterdam sits at $525-560/t (mid $542.50, 03-Jul), down from $600-625 in mid-May as the Middle East war premium receded - a move Brent's break below $100 extends. The floor beneath it is structural: the 6% EU import duty, CBAM and idled European capacity, with Mozal still in care & maintenance. Red Sea escalation is the offsetting risk for Suez-routed units.
drivers.source: S&P Global - European aluminum market seeks floor as Middle East war premium fades (07-Jul-2026)

notes: The alumina market remains the mirror image of metal: globally LOOSENING (EGA's 2.4 Mtpa restart at full output since 10-Jul, record Guinean bauxite exports, Chinese port stocks building; SMM Alumina Index easing toward ~Y2,700/t) - ex-China consolidation sits at ~$300-322 (FOB Australia ~$322, down from the $325-328 transacted early-July range).

The regional wrinkle persists but keeps easing: the shipping disruption still spans two waterways (a strained Hormuz plus Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea), yet the war-risk cover embedded in the ~60% of Gulf alumina imports that transit Hormuz is re-pricing lower as Brent broke $100 on 24-Jul and a US-Iran diplomacy track was floated. SMM separately flags ex-China metallurgical-grade output down ~6% y/y in June.

The ore leg has gone the other way from the bull case: Guinea's H1-2026 exports hit a RECORD 114.8 Mt (+15% y/y), with China taking 82.57 Mt Jan-May (+24% y/y). Guinea's pending export-quota policy (a considered cap near 150 Mt for 2026, targeting >$100/dmt) remains undecreed, and the record H1 flow materially weakens the case for it biting in 2026.

logistics.label: Strait of Hormuz transit
logistics.note: Hormuz traffic stays strained after a run of tanker interdictions and the US military says the waterway 'remains open with American support', but the direction of travel changed over the weekend: the US paused strikes to let diplomacy develop and Iran-Oman deputy-FM talks in Tehran on shared principles and operational mechanisms for safe passage were reported as constructive, with progress made. The US blockade of Iranian ports remains in effect. Roughly 80-85% of Gulf aluminium exports and ~60% of regional alumina imports use this route; ~9% of global primary supply sits behind the strait, so a working mechanism is the single largest potential supply release.

logistics.label: Red Sea corridor
logistics.note: Houthis struck two Saudi oil tankers (Encelia, Layla) in the Red Sea, and Asian buyers have begun rerouting Saudi crude via the Suez Canal and around Africa. The alternative-to-Hormuz corridor for Gulf exports is itself a war-risk zone - a second maritime chokepoint under active attack.

logistics.label: Gulf / Red Sea war-risk insurance
logistics.note: War-risk quotes stay elevated with two fronts in play, but the premium is easing at the margin: Brent settled $98.38 on 24-Jul (-2.29%) off the $100+ spike, and the weekend brought a US pause in strikes plus constructive Iran-Oman talks on Hormuz safe passage. Retain elevated insurance, interdiction and deviation-risk assumptions in Gulf- and Red Sea-routed freight and delivered-cost models, but the skew on that cost line has turned lower for the first time in weeks.

logistics.label: Baltic Dry Index (BDI)
logistics.note: Dry-bulk freight (a separate, slower-moving cost line) eased to ~2,671 on 20-Jul, down 81 points and off a mid-month peak near 2,944 on softer Capesize demand. Price the two legs separately: dry-bulk freight vs. the Gulf/Red Sea war-risk surcharge (Trading Economics / Baltic Exchange).

logistics.label: Land-bridge / alt routes (Gulf, Kazakh oil)
logistics.note: The overland-to-Red-Sea contingency is less clean with the Red Sea under attack. Separately, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium suspended loadings at its Black Sea terminal after tanker attacks, disrupting ~80% of Kazakhstan's oil exports - a reminder that alternative routes are also under stress. Keep carrier capacity and lead times current for any Gulf-origin cargo.

logistics.label: Incoterms / demurrage
logistics.note: Attacks spanning two waterways keep force-majeure and deviation clauses live for any Gulf- or Red Sea-routed cargo; war-risk surcharge pass-through and interdiction/delay risk remain live contract points to negotiate cargo-by-cargo. Generic supply-chain observation, not company-specific.

row.label: Brent crude
row.note: SETTLED $98.38 on 24-Jul, -2.29% (previous $100.69), having traded intraday to ~$96.8 - a clear break of the $100+ spike as US-Iran off-ramp reporting built. The weekend cut both ways: a specific Hormuz transit compromise is reportedly under negotiation (bearish), while Houthi strikes on Aramco facilities at Yanbu and Jizan and the Bab el-Mandeb closure threat are bullish. Energy is the largest smelter cost line - the fading spike is modest cost relief for European and Asian smelters. (Trading Economics)

headlines.title: The Hormuz off-ramp became specific. A regional official involved in the mediation says the compromise now being negotiated centres on Iran running vessel transit through the Strait with fewer restrictions on ships, and that both the US and Iran want to return to the interim ceasefire. US strikes paused after 13 consecutive nights, and Iran-Oman deputy-FM technical talks in Tehran were reported as progressing. The US naval blockade of Iranian ports remains enforced. A working transit mechanism is the main downside trigger for the war-risk premium in both flat price and regional premiums.

The second chokepoint escalated. After Saudi airstrikes on Hodeida, Yemen's Houthis fired missiles and drones at Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Jizan on Saturday and reiterated that they will close Bab el-Mandeb to Saudi-linked shipping - a corridor carrying roughly 12% of world trade that became more important for Gulf exports precisely because Hormuz was disrupted. Shipping and war-risk cost is migrating between waterways rather than clearing.

The 24-Jul official widened the cash-3M backwardation to +$14.50 from +$12.00 while LME stock drew an accelerated 2,400 t to 272,775 t - a fresh low since 2022 and ~-46.4% YTD - with SHFE also falling. A falling flat price alongside a widening backwardation and faster draws points to headline-driven length exiting a market that is physically tightening. Today's ring is the first test of whether price re-couples with the curve.

New US primary capacity is being commissioned behind the tariff wall. Commerce and South Carolina officials marked Century Aluminum's Mt Holly expansion on 23-Jul, publicly framed as lifting total US domestic primary aluminium output by roughly 10%, while Magnitude 7 Metals is restarting part of the New Madrid smelter in Missouri (~75 kt/y). Added domestic units are a medium-term drag on the residual US market premium, though not on the Section-232 tariff leg itself.
headlines.source: GlobeNewswire / US Dept of Commerce release (23-Jul-2026)

headlines.title: The ex-China alumina surplus keeps building: Platts FOB Australia futures are around $309/t and SMM-referenced FOB Western Australia spot near $322/t, easing as EGA's Al Taweelah refinery ramps back after a three-and-a-half-month outage. Cheaper feedstock lowers the marginal cost floor under the metal price.
headlines.source: TradingView (Alumina FOB Australia Platts futures) / S&P Global

headlines.title: Guinea's H1-2026 bauxite exports hit a record 114.8 Mt, up 15% y/y from 99.8 Mt, on robust Chinese demand; China imported 82.57 Mt of Guinean ore Jan-May (+24% y/y, ~82% of its total imports). Record seaborne length on the ore leg weakens the bullish read on the still-undecreed export-cap policy.

The SHFE/LME price ratio recovered, sharply narrowing the export margins that drove record H1 semis exports (June 711 kt; H1 +16.3% y/y). New orders are softening and semis-export flow faces reduction risk if margins stay compressed - a potential loosening of the export valve. Q2 GDP grew 4.3%, below the 4.5% consensus.

forward.basis: LME official prices via Westmetall. Baseline = LME 3-month official (a traded market price). Range = random-walk cone from realized volatility. Driver score = 3 transparent rules, hit rate measured on history.
forward.source: London Metal Exchange official settlements via Westmetall (https://www.westmetall.com/en/markdaten.php?action=table&field=LME_Al_cash)
forward.stance_label: Current physical-market condition (diagnostic, not a forecast)

drivers.name: Curve carry (cash − 3M)
drivers.rule: Backwardation (cash above 3M) = prompt physical tightness = bullish; contango = bearish.

drivers.name: Inventory trend (13-week)
drivers.rule: LME stock falling more than 2% over 13 weeks = tightening = bullish; rising >2% = bearish.

drivers.name: Momentum (3M vs 20-week average)
drivers.rule: Price above its 20-week average = uptrend = bullish; below = bearish.

backtest.verdict: These condition indicators showed NO predictive edge when tested: a 39.6% directional hit rate against a 73.3% naive 'always higher' baseline over the same sample, and forward returns after 'tightening' readings averaged 2.31% versus 7.04% after 'loosening' readings. They are therefore published as a read on CURRENT market condition only — not as a price forecast. The forward baseline and probability range above are the forward-looking view.
backtest.caveat: Measured on overlapping 13-week windows of weekly LME data (96 observations, 2024-05-24 to 2026-04-24). Overlapping windows overstate significance and the sample spans a single, largely rising market — evidence in either direction is weak.

earnings.note: Q2 2026 BEAT: adjusted EBITDA NOK 8,923m (+14.5% y/y vs NOK 7,790m; above consensus); Aluminium Metal adjusted EBITDA NOK 6,421m; adjusted EPS NOK 2.2 (from NOK 1.7); free cash flow NOK 4bn; 12-month adjusted RoaCE 10.9%. Shares rose on the print. First European producer P&L of the Hormuz-disruption quarter. Higher aluminium prices and product premiums plus stronger recycling earnings drove the beat; a stronger NOK and lower hydro-power output were partial offsets. Confirms the disruption-quarter price/premium is translating into real producer margin - a positive read-across for the smelter complex.

June-quarter production report: Worsley alumina 943 kt, Hillside aluminium 179 kt; group beat FY26 production guidance with quarterly sales +15%. Sale of the aluminium value chain to Alcoa (announced 01-Jul) progressing. Upstream volumes intact and above guidance; the aluminium/alumina divestment to Alcoa repositions S32 as an upstream base-metals play. Confirms Western supply is expressing the Gulf disruption through price/freight, not lost tonnage.

Revenue $3.97bn (+24% q/q, highest in nearly a decade); adj. EPS $2.12 (MISS vs ~$2.31 consensus); adj. net income $562m; adj. EBITDA $901m (from $595m in Q1); Aluminum segment RECORD EBITDA $1.073bn at 32.3% margin. First producer P&L under the Hormuz-disruption regime: record aluminium margins and near-decade-high revenue on higher LME + strong US Midwest premiums, but adj. EPS missed on higher costs — notably ~$35m more Section-232 tariff on Canadian metal into the US — and the shares fell. South32 upstream acquisition ($4.1bn upfront, up to $5.6bn contingent to 2030) progressing, close expected H1-2027. The tariff is a double edge: it inflates US premia but taxes Alcoa's cross-border Canadian metal.

Q2 2026 production (14-Jul): aluminium 841 kt (flat y/y, +1% q/q); bauxite recovered from Q1 weather; alumina reduced q/q on Yarwun/Vaudreuil reliability events; group aluminium guidance intact 3.25-3.45 Mt. Kitimat, NZAS and AP60 continued their ramp-up while Arvida's final two potlines closed in June as planned, completing the transition to AP60. Steady low-carbon Canadian output into a tight, premium-rich market - constructive for realised margins even as the flat price eased.

Guides H1-26 net profit ¥1.8–1.95bn, +154.4–175.6% YoY. Credits industry-chain cost reduction, aluminium prices fluctuating at highs, high-value-added deep-processing mix and energy-saving retrofits — the first sizeable China H1 pre-announcement of the season and a positive read-across for Chinese producer margins.

Hindalco PAT ₹5,283cr (+66% YoY); India Al upstream EBITDA margin ~46%; Novelis FY26 adj. EBITDA $1.6bn (−9%). Record India operations; Novelis pressured by Oswego outage (~$104m) and tariffs (~$143m).

Net profit $200.3m (+316% YoY); EPS 53 fils; sales −17% on Gulf supply-chain disruption. LME averaged $3,195/t (+22% YoY) drove profit surge; volumes hit by regional conflict; ~19% capacity in controlled shutdown — restart path improves post-truce.
Adj. EPS $1.63 (beat $1.56); revenue $649m; net income $327m (incl. $288m Hawesville sale gain). Higher LME + strong US Midwest premiums; Q2 adj. EBITDA guided $315–335m.

Net profit SAR 1.63bn (~$436m, +5.5% YoY); revenue SAR 8.79bn (+3.2%); EBITDA $964m. Strong pricing across commodities; partly offset by lower phosphate volumes; 2026 capex set >$4bn. Ma'aden (1211) reports Q2 2026 on 06-Aug-2026; the Q1 print remains the latest public result.
Net profit guided RMB 5.30–5.59bn (+50–58% YoY). Strong on higher Al prices; China output near self-imposed 45 Mt capacity cap.
FY25 net loss $455m (vs $803m profit in 2024) on higher costs & lower output. Analysts expect stronger H1 2026 on higher prices; Asia pivot amid fractured trade flows.
FY25 results; copper & aluminium average prices +9% YoY; zinc metal +4%. Resilient structural demand for Cu/Al cited; broadly constructive sector tone.
Underlying profit $6.2bn (+>20%); underlying EBITDA $15.5bn (+25%, 58% margin); interim div 73c. Copper-led strength; broad base-metals read-across positive for the complex.

catalysts.text: Today's LME official (13:20 London) - the first price to see the weekend on both waterways. caveats: Report refreshed Mon 27-Jul-2026, ~06:05 London - BEFORE the LME ring. The benchmark table and lme_series carry the latest PUBLISHED LME aluminium official, which is the 24-Jul (Friday) settlement: cash $3,175.00 / 3M $3,160.50 / stock 272,775 t, from Westmetall, re-verified against the source at this refresh. The exchange was closed Saturday and Sunday; today's official prints 13:20 London. This official therefore PRE-DATES the weekend developments described below entirely - no price in this report reflects them.

BOARD BASIS IS UNIFORM: aluminium, copper, nickel, zinc and lead are all set to their LME 24-Jul 3-month officials (Westmetall), each re-verified this run - a single, consistent session across the whole board. Spot/CFD references (Trading Economics) are a different basis from officials and will not tie out exactly: the traded aluminium reference closed $3,165.05 on 24-Jul against the official 3M of $3,160.50, and Trading Economics' nickel ($17,310) and zinc ($3,589.65) differ from the LME officials shown.

YTD FIGURES ON THE BOARD are computed against each metal's first-published 2026 LME 3-month official (aluminium: $3,010.50 on 02-Jan-2026) and are indicative, not exchange-published index returns. Aluminium's -46.4% YTD stock change is measured from 509,250 t on 02-Jan-2026.

GEOPOLITICAL DEVELOPMENTS ARE FAST-MOVING and now materially post-date the settled 24-Jul official, having moved in BOTH directions over the weekend. Downside: a regional official involved in the mediation says the compromise being negotiated centres on Iran running vessel transit through Hormuz with fewer restrictions on ships, with both the US and Iran wanting back to the interim ceasefire, US strikes paused after 13 consecutive nights, and Iran-Oman technical talks progressing. Upside: Houthi missiles and drones struck Aramco facilities at Yanbu and Jizan after Saudi strikes on Hodeida, with Bab el-Mandeb restated as closed to Saudi-linked shipping. No agreement has been signed and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports remains enforced. Treat the flat price as lagging the news flow, and note the internal divergence flagged throughout: price fell while the backwardation widened and draws accelerated.

PREMIUM ASSESSMENTS ARE PERIODIC, NOT DAILY: MJP settles quarterly (Q3 $395/t, 06-Jul); Rotterdam duty-unpaid ($542.50, 03-Jul) and US Midwest (108.7-112 c/lb, 03-10 Jul) are assessed by Platts/Fastmarkets/SMM on their own schedules and no fresher public prints have appeared. The tariff/market decomposition IS refreshed every run because it is a function of the current LME cash. Figures shown are the latest PUBLIC prints, not daily marks.

THE SECTION-232 RATE WAS RE-VERIFIED THIS RUN and is unchanged: 50% on articles made entirely or almost entirely of aluminium, 25% on derivative aluminium content, effective 08-Jun-2026 through 31-Dec-2027 per the 01-Jun-2026 proclamation (CBP guidance CSMS #68855869).
